articles.title: Young Adults Find It Difficult to Make Friends — Survey
articles.intro: Explore why many young adults in the US find it difficult to make friends, based on survey results and social factors affecting connections.

sentences.text: As kids, making a friend was as easy as sitting next to somebody in class, or playing a game together on the playground.
But it's not the same for adults.
In fact, a survey has found that 69% of US young adults feel lonelier than they ever thought they would.
The survey was done by Talker Research, and included 1,000 Gen Z participants — defined as those born between 1997 and 2008.
It found that the average participant feels lonely four days a week, and 52% find it difficult to make new connections.
Forty-three percent of participants said they have fewer than three close friends.
And one in six said they only see those friends a few times a year.
So why are US young adults struggling to make friends?
Many said it's because going out and meeting people is expensive.
Others said they're too tired after work, or are too busy in other parts of their lives.
The survey also found that 60% of participants think they don't have a regular place to meet people and make friends.
This is sometimes called a "third space" — a place outside the home or work where people can spend time together.
But almost 60% also said they see the place where they work out as a "third space."
And that could be something they might want to look into if they're looking to make friends.
So maybe for young adults, making friends can still be as easy as meeting people on the playground — the playground just looks a little different.

articles.title: US Parents Say Having a Baby Is Too Expensive
articles.intro: This lesson discusses how many US parents feel the cost of raising a child is too high and explores their views on possible solutions.

sentences.text: A new baby is a cause for happiness and celebration.
But a baby also comes with large costs, from diapers and formula to car seats and childcare.
A survey by the University of Michigan found that four out of five American parents think the cost of having a baby is now just too high.
The survey included around 2,000 US adults who are parents of at least one child aged zero to 18.
Nearly all parents included in the survey agreed that early development is important to a child's long-term health.
However, giving a child what they need at a young age has often meant parents need to cut their spending, work extra hours or use secondhand items.

The survey found that parents of younger children are especially affected by the cost of having kids, with two in five describing their family's financial situation as either "struggling" or "just getting by."
And 37% of parents in these two groups said they worry about money all the time.

A lot of parents of older children haven't forgotten how difficult the first few years can be though, with 38% saying they have donated to organizations to help families with young children in the past two years.
Many parents would also support government programs to make things easier for new parents.
Three in four support the idea of a state program to give paid leave during pregnancy and during the first few weeks or months of a baby's life.

Six in 10 also said they would support programs to give families in need baby formula or healthy food, while more than half support the idea of free or lower-cost childcare, as well as free car seats and diapers.

articles.title: 'Maxxing' Named Dictionary.com's Word of the Year
articles.intro: Explore the rise of "maxxing" as Dictionary.com's Word of the Year, its meanings, examples, and societal impact.

sentences.text: Trying to get more sleep, eat more protein or look your best?
There's now a word for taking each of those goals to the extreme: "maxxing."
And the trend has become so popular that Dictionary.com has named it its Word of the Year for 2026.
Short for "maximizing," maxxing means doing something to the fullest, or trying to make one part of your life as good as possible.
It can be used on its own, but is usually added to another word.
So, "looksmaxxing" is about improving your appearance, while "sleepmaxxing" means trying to get better rest.
At work, "tokenmaxxing" means using as much AI as possible.
Even spending a quiet evening at home can become "cozymaxxing."
While the term has been around in different forms for a long time, it's the rise of "looksmaxxing" that brought it into wider use and helped popularize the spelling with an extra "x."
According to Steve Johnson, Dictionary.com's director of lexicography, its use in the media has risen by more than 1,000% since the start of 2026.
To choose its Word of the Year, Dictionary.com looks at how often a word appears in news articles, on social media and in online searches.
But the team also looks for a word that captures something distinctive about the year.
Johnson believes "maxxing" captures the pressure many people feel, especially online, to keep doing more and becoming better at everything, from work and school to health and appearance.
"If there is an aspect of life that could be improved, it can probably be maxxed," health researcher Jennifer Donnelly wrote in _The Conversation_.
But Donnelly warns that the constant drive for self-improvement can also lead to unrealistic expectations and stress.
Other words Dictionary.com considered for this year's title included "affordability," "data center," and "{{prn:unc|unk}}" — a shortened form of "uncle" used to refer to an uncool older adult.

articles.title: The Story of Mexico's _Dia de los Muertos_
articles.intro: Explore the history, traditions, and cultural significance of Mexico’s Día de los Muertos, including its indigenous and Spanish influences.

sentences.text: Orange flowers fill the streets, candles light up family altars and sugar skulls appear in shops — this is Mexico's _Dia de los Muertos_, or "Day of the Dead."
People often confuse this celebration with Halloween, but the Day of the Dead has its own unique traditions and history.
It takes place over two days — typically November 1 and November 2 — and it's a time to honor deceased loved ones.
This holiday has roots in Indigenous traditions that may date as far back as the Olmec civilization over 3,000 years ago.

These early practices were passed down through later civilizations like the Maya and the Toltecs until they reached the Aztecs — who believed that, after death, the soul travels to an underworld called Mictlan.
This journey could be long and difficult, and the dead needed help from their loved ones to reach Mictlan.
Families would leave offerings of food, water and personal belongings when a loved one died, to help guide the spirits and honor them.
In the 16th century, Spanish colonizers arrived in Mexico, bringing with them new religious traditions.
In Catholicism, November 1 is All Saints' Day — a day to honor all the saints who have reached heaven — while November 2 is All Souls' Day, a day to remember and pray for people who have died.
Over time, elements of these different traditions came together, making _Dia de los Muertos_ an important part of Mexican culture.
Every year in towns and cities across Mexico, the streets are decorated with flowers and skeletons, and people paint their faces to look like skulls.
Many families build _ofrendas_ in their homes or by the graves of their loved ones.
An _ofrenda_ is a type of altar decorated with candles, flowers and photos of the deceased, as well as some of their favorite items and foods.

Families believe these offerings help welcome the spirits of their loved ones back for a visit, making _Dia de los Muertos_ a celebration of life and the memories that keep people connected, even after death.

articles.title: One in Four European Pilots Fly When Tired
articles.intro: Explore survey findings on European airline pilots flying while fatigued, the risks involved, and the impact of company culture on safety reporting.

sentences.text: Getting through a workday feeling tired can be difficult for anyone.
But for airline pilots, it can become a serious safety issue.
A new survey of about 7,200 European pilots found that nearly one in four usually keep flying even when they feel too tired to work.
The survey was done by aviation safety company Baines Simmons for the European Cockpit Association.
It found that fatigue is a common problem across European airlines, with little change since 2023, when a similar survey was done.
More than three-quarters of pilots said they'd had at least one "microsleep" while flying in the past four weeks, with one-quarter saying they'd had five or more.
A microsleep is a very short, unintentional moment of sleep.
Not getting enough rest is a big part of the problem.

Thirty-nine percent of pilots said they "usually" or "always" had too little rest to stop fatigue from building up, while more than half said they had flown in the past three months and later realized they should have reported themselves too tired to fly.
In fact, only 37% said they usually let management know when they feel too tired to fly.
One reason may be fear of how airlines will react.
Almost half of pilots said they had flown while fatigued because they were worried about reactions from management.
The survey also found big differences between airlines and countries, with pilots at low-cost airlines reporting more problems.

Those working for airlines in Ireland and Malta were among the most likely to fear negative reactions from management, while Finland and the Netherlands had some of the strongest fatigue-reporting cultures.
The European Cockpit Association said airlines and aviation authorities need to do more to reduce fatigue risks, instead of leaving pilots to manage them on their own.

articles.title: Chinese Carmakers Overtake Japanese Rivals in Europe
articles.intro: This lesson explores how Chinese carmakers have surpassed Japanese rivals in European sales, market trends, and the impact on global automotive competition.

sentences.text: Chinese carmakers have overtaken Japanese brands in European sales for the first time over a full quarter, marking a major shift in the region's automotive market.

According to market research firm Dataforce, Chinese brands accounted for {{prn:12.7%|twelve point seven percent}} of new-car registrations between July and September 2026, compared with {{prn:11.9%|eleven point nine percent}} for Japanese manufacturers including Toyota, Nissan and Honda.
Registrations of Chinese cars roughly doubled year on year, with their market share hitting a record 14.5% in September, up almost three percentage points from August.
Just five years ago, Chinese brands held barely 1% of the European market.
Japanese manufacturers, meanwhile, have spent several decades establishing themselves there.
Toyota, for example, has sold cars in Europe since 1963.
Much of China's surge has been driven by competitively priced hybrid vehicles, which have become increasingly appealing to European buyers as fuel prices rise.
Brands such as BYD and Chery have been particularly successful.
In the UK, Chery's Jaecoo 7 SUV was the country's best-selling car in both March and September.
And while European manufacturers still dominate the region, competition is intensifying in Europe, as well as in China.
In what has traditionally been one of the biggest markets for European carmakers, buyers in China are increasingly choosing domestically made vehicles.

On October 29, Volkswagen reported a {{prn:$6.6 billion|six point six billion dollars}} third-quarter loss, compared with {{prn:$1.2 billion|one point two billion dollars}} a year earlier — its worst quarterly result in more than a decade.
The results add pressure as Volkswagen restructures to cut costs.
The company plans to eliminate up to 100,000 jobs by 2030, while four of its German factories face possible closure.
"We cannot afford to lose any time.
We must act quickly and decisively," said Volkswagen's finance chief, Arno Antlitz.
Meanwhile, the European Union has introduced additional tariffs on Chinese-made electric vehicles and is considering further restrictions on hybrid imports.
It's also weighing new rules that would favor locally manufactured cars when awarding subsidies and other incentives.
However, Chinese manufacturers are already preparing to produce more cars in Europe.
BYD is nearing completion of a factory in Hungary, while Chery is preparing production in Barcelona, Spain.

articles.title: Patrick Stewart, Legendary 'Star Trek' Actor, Dies at 86
articles.intro: This lesson explores the life, career, and legacy of Patrick Stewart, famed for Star Trek and X-Men, including his achievements on stage and screen.

sentences.text: Patrick Stewart, the British actor best known for playing Captain Jean-Luc Picard in _Star Trek_ and Professor Charles Xavier in the _X-Men_ films, has died at 86.
Stewart died on October 28 in Los Angeles, following a brief battle with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia.
"We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today," his _X-Men_ co-star Hugh Jackman wrote on social media.
"And, in my book, a tremendous friend and man."
Although Stewart became famous for his screen roles, he spent much of his career onstage.
Born in Mirfield, Yorkshire, in northern England, Stewart grew up in a working-class family, and later spoke openly about witnessing domestic violence as a child.
He joined an amateur drama group at 12 and developed a love for Shakespeare.
"The stage would prove to be a safe space, a refuge from real life in which I could inhabit another person, living in another place and time," he later wrote.
He attended the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School and spent 14 years with the Royal Shakespeare Company, performing in numerous Shakespeare plays.
Stewart's television breakthrough came in 1987 with _Star Trek: The Next Generation._
He initially expected the series to fail, but instead, it ran for seven seasons and 178 episodes, followed by four feature films.
His Shakespearean training helped him portray the starship commander, whose formal manner reminded him of characters he had played onstage.
In 2000, Stewart appeared as Professor Charles Xavier in the first _X-Men_ film.
He continued playing the character in several more movies, including 2017's _Logan_ and 2022's _Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness._
Throughout his career, Stewart continued working in theater, earning three Olivier Awards and a Tony Award nomination for _Macbeth_.
He also won a Grammy in 1996 for his spoken-word recording of _Peter and the Wolf._
He was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in 2010.
Stewart also became popular with younger audiences through his humor and social media posts.
He appeared in _The Simpsons_, _Futurama_ and _The Emoji Movie_.
Stewart is survived by his wife, singer and songwriter Sunny Ozell, whom he married in 2013, and his two children.

articles.title: What Do British People Complain About Most?
articles.intro: Explore what British people complain about most in public, from rude behavior to everyday annoyances and survey findings.

sentences.text: What annoys you most when you're out in public?
People being rude?
Someone pushing ahead of you in a line?
Or perhaps someone using their phone's speaker in public?
A new survey shows that British people have a lot to complain about.
The survey, done by YouGov, asked more than 2,000 people across the UK what bothers them about other people when they're in public.
The biggest complaint was people being rude to shop and restaurant workers, which annoys 67% of people who took the survey.
People who don't wait their turn in a line came second, at 59%.
Other common problems included people using their phone speakers in public, people taking up too much space on streets or buses and trains, and people making videos of themselves for social media.
But while these things bother people, they aren't actually the things they complain about most.
In fact, when asked what they complain about most in everyday life, 24% chose things they see in the news.
Another 18% chose people being rude — so that's on both lists — while 11% chose work.
And although British people are famous for talking about the country's bad weather, only 6% said the weather was what they complain about most.
And just 8% chose traffic.
Overall, 76% said they were people who often complain, while 20% said they never do.
And of the complainers, almost half said they usually share their problems with family or a partner, instead of speaking to the person who upset them.

articles.title: Japan's Budget Restaurant Saizeriya Raises Prices
articles.intro: This lesson discusses why Japanese restaurant chain Saizeriya raised prices, including rising costs and efforts to stay affordable for customers.

sentences.text: With food prices rising around the world, finding a cheap meal isn't always easy.
But in Japan, one restaurant chain is famous for keeping its prices low.

Saizeriya, a popular Italian restaurant chain, sells its famous Milano doria for just 300 yen (about {{prn:$1.90|one dollar and ninety cents}}), while a Margherita pizza costs only 400 yen (about {{prn:$2.50|two dollars and fifty cents}}).
Or at least, that's what they used to cost.
But now, Saizeriya is increasing its prices for the first time in six years.
On October 29, Saizeriya prices increased by an average of 6%, and some restaurants increased prices by as much as 10%.
It's the company's first general price increase since 1998.
Saizeriya did make some small changes in 2020, but those were intended to reduce the need for coins and change during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Over the years, Saizeriya has found different ways to save money and keep its prices low.
For example, it has its own vegetable farms and factories, and has even tried using robots to serve food.
But these efforts are no longer enough, as higher food and energy costs have made it difficult to avoid price increases.
At a press conference in October, Saizeriya CEO Hideharu Matsutani said the price increase was "regrettable."
But after hearing the announcement, many people shared messages on social media in support of Saizeriya.

One customer told _The Japan Times_ that Saizeriya's meals have been so cheap that eating there can cost less than cooking at home, and that most people are just surprised the company has kept its prices so low for so long.
And even with the higher prices, Saizeriya still wants to keep its food affordable.
At the press conference, Matsutani said that if the company finds another way to make meals cheaper, he'll take it.

articles.title: Japan Struggles to Respond to Cascade of Data Leaks
articles.intro: Explore Japan's recent wave of cyberattacks, massive data leaks, their causes, and expert recommendations for better security practices.

sentences.text: A cascade of cyberattacks on Japanese companies and other organizations in recent weeks has resulted in massive data leaks that have exposed the personal information of millions of people — with some companies reporting that almost their entire user bases may have been exposed.

Just since September, affected companies have included everything from Bookoff Group Holdings — which runs the popular Bookoff used bookstore chain — to popular shipping company Yamato Transport, better known as Kuroneko.
Potentially compromised data has included names, phone numbers, email addresses, mailing addresses, birth dates, parts of credit card numbers — even driver's licenses.
On October 26, the Japanese government held an urgent meeting to discuss the problem, and announced that emergency measures would be decided on by the end of next week.
But just a day later, Japanese internet company GMO Internet said an attacker had published private information from one of its services that provides virtual desktops for financial traders.
A week earlier, GMO had said it had found evidence that an AI-enabled security testing tool called Artex had been used in hacks targeting companies across Japan.
Experts say the attacks aren't particularly sophisticated, however — rather, they're exploiting basic security weaknesses in consumer-facing services that can be accessed through the internet.
"Most cases involve the exploitation of known vulnerabilities or configuration errors," Hiroaki Kuramochi of Tokyo-based cybersecurity company Lac Co. told _The Asahi Shimbun_.
"It feels as though AI is now catching configuration errors that humans previously overlooked."

However, Kuramochi also said companies should assume it's impossible to stop every data breach — and they should instead focus on reducing the amount of data that can be lost to a leak, by saving only the personal information that's truly important for their services, and only keeping that information as long as it's needed.

Japan's Minister for Digital Transformation Toshiharu Furukawa has also recommended that users should stop using the same password across different accounts, and should be sure to use multi-factor authentication, which verifies a person's identity using more than just a single password.

articles.title: Apple Unveils Its First Touchscreen Laptop
articles.intro: Explore Apple's first touchscreen MacBook, its features, market impact, creative uses, and Apple’s approach to adopting new technology.

sentences.text: For years, Apple dismissed the idea of touchscreen laptops. In 2010, co-founder Steve Jobs called them "ergonomically terrible."
Two years later, then-CEO Tim Cook compared combining a laptop and a tablet to putting a toaster and a refrigerator together.
Now, Apple has changed course.
"Yes, for the very first time, we are bringing touch to the Mac," Apple CEO John Ternus announced at an event in Los Angeles on October 28.

The new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display comes in 14-inch and 16-inch versions, with US prices starting at {{prn:$2,899|two thousand eight hundred and ninety nine dollars}} and {{prn:$3,399|three thousand three hundred and ninety nine dollars}} respectively.

Users can still control it with a keyboard and trackpad, but can now also scroll through webpages, pinch to zoom in on photos, drag slides between presentations and move windows around with their fingers.
Apple says many existing apps will work with the touchscreen immediately because the software automatically treats taps as mouse clicks.
The technology could be particularly useful for creative professionals.
Graphic designers can draw directly on the screen, musicians can play virtual instruments, and app developers can test touch controls in iPhone and iPad apps.
Touchscreen laptops have been around for over a decade.
While early models were often bulky and awkward to use, the technology has since improved significantly.
The market is growing, too.
According to research firm IDC, around 33.4 million touchscreen laptops were shipped worldwide in 2025, up 22% from the previous year.
However, they still accounted for only 16% of all laptop shipments.
And Apple is no stranger to entering a market late.
It wasn't the first to introduce MP3 players, tablets or smartwatches, but helped popularize them through simpler, more intuitive designs.
The touchscreen MacBook is the latest in a series of products announced since Ternus became CEO in September.
Under the former head of hardware engineering, Apple has also unveiled the foldable iPhone Duo and HomeView, a smart-home hub.
The new MacBook Pro is now available for pre-order and will go on sale on November 6.

articles.title: Tea May Benefit Heart Health — If It's Not Too Hot
articles.intro: This lesson explores how tea consumption may lower the risk of heart disease and stroke, and how drinking temperature can influence its effects.

sentences.text: Regular tea drinking may be linked to a lower risk of heart disease and stroke, according to a new study from China.
But how hot you drink it could matter, too!
Researchers looked at data from almost 486,000 people in China aged between 30 and 79.
Participants reported how often they drank tea, which type they preferred, how strong they brewed it and how hot they drank it.
The study, published in the _Journal of Internal Medicine_, tracked their health for an average of nine years.
People who drank tea on at least three days a week had an 11% lower risk of vascular disease — including heart disease and stroke — than those who drank it less often.
The link remained after the researchers considered factors such as age, smoking, physical activity, body weight and existing health conditions.
Black tea was more consistently associated with a lower risk of vascular disease than green tea, although both were associated with benefits.
Moderate-strength tea was also linked with a lower risk.
However, those who described their tea as "burning hot" had a 16% higher risk of vascular disease than people who did not regularly drink tea.
The temperatures were reported by participants, rather than measured by the researchers.
Tea contains polyphenols, which may help explain these findings.
These plant compounds may help reduce inflammation, protect the cells lining blood vessels and keep arteries working well.
However, the study doesn't prove that tea caused the differences in risk.
Other differences in people's diets and lifestyles could help explain the results.
In fact, the lowest risk of vascular disease was found among regular tea drinkers who also did not smoke and had high levels of physical activity.
So although tea may have benefits for your health, it should be considered just one part of a generally healthy lifestyle.

articles.title: Sauce on the Side Makes a Meal Look Healthier — Study
articles.intro: A study shows that serving sauce on the side makes a meal appear healthier, even though taste and enjoyment stay the same.

sentences.text: The way a meal looks may affect how healthy we think it is — and as one study found, it can be as simple as where you put the sauce.
The research was done by a team from Keio University in Japan, who set up a restaurant in Tokyo's Nihonbashi neighborhood and invited 57 guests to dine there.
Each participant was asked to evaluate two versions of the same sturgeon-fritter dish.
One had its sauces drizzled across the food and the plate, while the other had the sauces just placed next to the food on the plate.
Before they ate, participants were asked to rate each version of the dish on how tasty it looked, how healthy it seemed and how much they wanted to try it.

Also, to make sure the results weren't affected by the order in which the dishes were served, half of the group started with the drizzled sauce version, while the other half started with the sauce-on-the-side version.
After eating each dish, they were asked the same questions as before, as well as how much they enjoyed it.
For the most part, participants rated both versions of the dish around the same for how tasty they looked, how much they wanted to try them, and how much they enjoyed them.
However, there was a small but notable difference in how healthy participants felt each dish was.
The dish presented with its sauces on the side got an average score for healthiness of 4.65 out of 7, while the drizzled sauce got an average score of 4.05.
The researchers suggest that the simpler presentation of having sauces on the side might make a dish seem more natural, and also gives diners control of how much sauce they eat.

articles.title: 27% of US Workers Using Savings to Cover Expenses
articles.intro: This lesson explores how rising living costs in the US are forcing many workers to use their savings to cover daily expenses and financial emergencies.

sentences.text: As the cost of living increases around the world, it's getting harder to save money while covering everyday expenses.

In September, a survey by Talker Research for financial technology company Chime found that 27% of US workers had had to unexpectedly withdraw money from their savings accounts in the previous 24 hours.
A little over one in 10 also said they'd had to take money out of their savings in just the last few hours before taking the survey.
The survey was done between September {{prn:3|third}} and September 8, and included {{prn:1,000|one thousand}} workers on a salary and {{prn:1,000|one thousand}} workers who earned an hourly wage.
And even though 84% of all workers said building up their savings was one of their top financial goals, there was a big difference between the two groups in how well they were able to do so.
Just 5% of workers with a salary said they'd needed to take money from their savings in the last few hours, while 20% of workers with an hourly wage said they'd had to do so.
The survey also found that 55% of hourly wage workers take money from their savings every week, using an average of $216 per month.
The money isn't always being taken out for big emergencies either, as 34% of hourly workers said they'd used their savings for things like groceries, medication and gas.
"Hourly workers aren't telling us they don't want to save.
They're telling us they can't keep their savings saved," said Bill Gartland from Chime.
"When money set aside for the future repeatedly has to cover groceries, medication or the days before payday, it becomes much harder to build a financial cushion," he said.

articles.title: New French Literary Prize Rewards Books Written with AI
articles.intro: Explore France’s new literary prize for AI-assisted books, entry rules, and the growing debate over AI’s role in major writing competitions.

sentences.text: A new literary prize in France will reward books written with the help of artificial intelligence.
The Prix Pascal de Littérature IA was started by three French technology entrepreneurs — Philippe Rodriguez, Albin Serviant and Gilles Mentré — and is open to anyone who writes in French.
To enter, writers must submit an unpublished work of fiction of between 10,000 and 50,000 words co-written with AI.
They can use any of the major AI tools, including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and more.
However, applicants have to be open about how they used the technology.
Along with their manuscript, they must submit the name of the AI model used, as well as the prompts and methods they used to create the story.
The organizers say the submitted works should in some way pertain to an ethical, social or ecological problem threatening humanity.
Applications opened on October 20, and will close at the end of November.
A jury of writers, critics, publishers, philosophers and journalists will choose 10 finalists before selecting a winner in early December.
The winning work will be published.
The prize comes as other literary competitions grapple with how to deal with AI.

In September, Canadian-Haitian writer Thélyson Orélien was removed from the longlist for France's most prestigious literary prize, the Prix Goncourt, amid allegations that he had used AI to write his novel, _It Was Either That or Die_.
The critically acclaimed book had already sold about 35,000 copies.
Orélien denied the claims, but his Canadian publisher later said it had confirmed that AI had been used in the writing process, and ended its relationship with him.
Other major writing prizes, including the Caine Prize for African writers and the Commonwealth Short Story Prize, have also faced allegations that winning entries were created with AI.
And in Japan, a 20-year-old short poetry competition ended in February after organizers said it had become too difficult to tell whether some entries had been written by humans or AI.

articles.title: Adults More Creative than Kids, Less Confident — Study
articles.intro: This lesson explores a study showing that adults are more creative but less confident than children, who are more motivated and enjoy creative tasks more.

sentences.text: Many people believe that young children are more creative than adults.
However, a recent study has found that it's adults who may actually be more creative — they're just less confident!
The study was published in _{{prn:PLOS|ploss}} One_, and included  92 preschool children and 70 adults, with 85% of the adults aged between 20 and 30 years old.
Each participant took part in the same three creative activities.
First, everyone was given a tin can and three minutes to think of how many ways they could use it.
Next, they all spent eight minutes drawing whatever they wanted with colored pens.
The researchers chose to make this part seem like it wasn't a test, and just a chance for participants to get used to the materials for the next part.
Finally, everyone used those same materials to spend another eight minutes inventing and drawing their own unique fantasy animal.
After these three tasks, the participants answered questions about how confident or anxious they felt, and how much they enjoyed the activities.
Trained judges then looked at the products from each task, from tin can ideas to fantasy masterpieces.
They actually found that adults' ideas were more original, effective and creative than what the children came up with.
The preschool children felt much better about their efforts, though — they enjoyed the tasks more, were more motivated and less anxious about their work than the adults.
Also, when asked, more than three-quarters of the adults in the study believed that the children were more creative than them.
The researchers think this may be because adults see children's enthusiasm and confidence as proof of their greater creativity.

The study also found that children take part in creative activities far more often than adults — an average of once a day versus once a week — which again could cause grown-ups to see children as more creative.

articles.title: Brits Now Track Four Health Habits a Day
articles.intro: Explore how people in the UK are increasingly tracking daily health habits like steps, sleep, water intake, and exercise, and the effects on lifestyle.

sentences.text: How many steps did you take today?
How many hours of sleep did you get?
And did you drink enough water?
For many people in the UK, checking numbers like these is now part of everyday life.
A new OnePoll survey of 2,000 adults found that the average Brit tracks four aspects of their health and lifestyle each day.
Steps, exercise and sleep were among the things people track the most.
But many are also looking at things like how much water and protein they're getting, their breathing rate and "body battery" — a measure some fitness devices use to show a person's energy levels.
Perhaps unsurprisingly, younger adults are tracking the most.
Those aged 45 and under track an average of five things a day, while those aged 62 and over track fewer than three.
And health tracking is only getting more popular.
Over the past five years, sleep tracking has more than doubled, increasing by {{prn:108%|one hundred and eight percent}}.
Counting daily steps has increased by 72%, while water tracking is up 65%.
Weight was the only measure to become less popular, though, with 3% fewer people tracking it.
All those numbers are having an impact — 43% of people said tracking had made them change something about their lifestyle.
Among them, 51% started walking more, 49% drank more water and 45% exercised more.

The survey also found that the average person in the UK walks {{prn:7,135|seven thousand one hundred and thirty five}} steps a day, gets about six and a half hours of sleep and drinks 1.2 liters of water.
And people do like hitting their targets!
Seven in ten said meeting their daily targets encourages them to keep up healthier habits.

articles.title: Many Young Adults Don't Have DIY Skills — Survey
articles.intro: This lesson explores a survey about young adults lacking traditional DIY skills but having strong digital abilities like setting up Wi-Fi and using AI.

sentences.text: Uh-oh.
You've taken out the plug in your sink but the water isn't going down.
Do you know how to fix it?
Or do you have to call for help?
According to a new survey from the UK, many young adults don't have basic DIY skills, and would probably have to call for help.
The survey was done by website hosting platform Tiiny Host, and included 2,000 British adults.
It found that nearly a third of 18-to-24-year-olds never do any home maintenance themselves, because they're afraid they'll make things worse.
Forty percent said they don't think they'd be able to hang a mirror, while nearly three-quarters said they wouldn't feel confident putting together flat-pack furniture.
Just under a quarter said they feel confident doing basic home maintenance, like putting up shelves.
But this doesn't mean young adults have no skills — they just have different skills.
Forty-one percent said they would have no problem setting up a home Wi-Fi network without help, and 36% said they know how to create a website.
And 80% of 18-to-25-year-olds said they'd used AI to create or help with projects.
In fact, the survey found that young adults are more likely to have created something with AI in the past year than to have put up a shelf in their home.
Tiiny Host founder Elston Baretto said DIY skills aren't disappearing — they're just changing.
In the past, DIY skills may have referred only to things like building furniture or painting a wall.
But Baretto said: "Today, that same instinct to create, learn and figure things out for yourself is increasingly happening online."
He added that this doesn't mean one set of skills matters more than the other — but young adults are still doing things for themselves, just in a different way.

articles.title: Airbnb Hosts Can No Longer Ask Guests to Clean
articles.intro: This lesson discusses Airbnb's new policy limiting hosts from asking guests to do extensive cleaning and outlines acceptable property rules.

sentences.text: It's the last day of your vacation.
But instead of enjoying your last few hours, you're busy washing the dishes and taking the sheets off the beds in your Airbnb.
Many Airbnb hosts ask guests to clean up before they check out.
If the guests don't clean, they may be given a bad review on the platform.
But hosts will no longer be able to ask guests to clean up, Airbnb has announced.
Airbnb guests are already required to pay a cleaning fee — which is usually included in the total price — and many guests have complained about having to clean up after themselves on top of that.

Now, Airbnb has said that, from November 20, hosts on the platform will no longer be able to ask guests to do things that "require significant effort or time," or that would usually be done by a cleaner.
So, for example, a host can ask their guests to put dirty dishes in the sink, but cannot ask them to wash them and put them away.
Airbnb has said that hosts can choose up to seven rules for their property.
These can include things like check in and check out times, how many guests can stay at the property, and whether or not people can smoke.
Guests must be told about these rules when they book the property.
Airbnb added that hosts can also make a number of "reasonable requests," such as not taking very long showers if water is scarce in the area.

articles.title: Americans May Eat More Processed Food than They Think
articles.intro: Explore how many Americans eat ultra-processed foods, related health risks, misconceptions, and the differences between processed and ultra-processed foods.

sentences.text: Diets high in ultra-processed foods (UPFs) have been linked with a number of health issues, including an increased risk of obesity, type 2 diabetes and heart disease.
But could people be eating even more UPFs than they realize?

A survey by Talker Research of 2,000 Americans for food brand Amy's Kitchen — which makes prepackaged meals like pizzas, soups and burritos — found that nine in 10 are likely eating UPFs without realizing it.
On average, survey participants reported that only 16% of their diets were made up of UPFs.

However, the researchers also looked at data from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, which said that 53% of the average US diet is UPFs — so people could be eating close to three times as many UPFs as they realize.
Even though 71% of participants said they think about the amount of UPFs in their diet, 61% said these foods are now so common they don't think they can avoid them.

And while it may be obvious that things like soda and potato chips are ultra-processed, a lot of common grocery items can be considered UPFs depending on their exact recipe and how they're made — including some sliced bread and breakfast cereals.
Some people might also get confused by foods and beverages that may be labeled as healthy despite also being highly processed, like some plant-based milks and protein bars.
Half of respondents also said they weren't confident they understood the difference between "processed" and "ultra-processed" at all.
This matters, because not all kinds of food processing make something a UPF or bad for you.
For example, pasteurizing milk makes it much safer.
And while freezing, fermenting and canning are all types of processing, they don't make food ultra-processed.

Yet one-third of participants said they believed any kind of processing made a food "bad," meaning they mistakenly believed things like canned or frozen vegetables were as unhealthy as chips or cookies!

articles.title: Young Japanese Have Worse Diets than Older Japanese
articles.intro: This lesson explores a study comparing the diets of young and older Japanese people, highlighting health, nutrition, and lifestyle factors.

sentences.text: A new study has found that young adults in Japan often have less healthy diets than older people in the country.
Researchers from the University of Tokyo did a study with about 4,500 people in Japan.
The people were as old as 79, and as young as just 1.
The researchers asked them — or their parents — to write down what they ate and drank for eight days.
Then, they gave them diet scores.
The researchers looked at two things: the foods people ate, like fruit and vegetables, and the nutrients they got, like vitamins.
Men who were around 23 years old, and women who were around 16, had the lowest scores for the foods they ate.
After that, their scores got better almost every year they got older.
For nutrients, both men's and women's scores went up until around age 10.
But then they went down quickly, until they were at their lowest around age 24.
After that, nutrient scores started slowly going up again.
The study also found that people from families with more money and education had healthier diets.
And smokers and people who skip breakfast in the morning had less healthy diets.
The researchers said teens and young adults may find it harder to eat well because their lives are changing so much at that age.
But they said it's important to teach young people how to eat healthily.

articles.title: Finland's 24/7 Puppy Livestream Draws Millions
articles.intro: Explore Finland’s popular 24/7 puppy livestream, its impact on viewers, and how “slow TV” brings joy and relaxation to millions.

sentences.text: Six newborn puppies in Finland are winning over millions of viewers with every little wiggle and squeak.
The puppies are the stars of _Pentulive_, a 24/7 livestream from Finland's public broadcaster Yle.
_Pentu_ means "puppy" in Finnish.
The four males and two females were born on October 10 to a 5-year-old Lagotto Romagnolo named Hilkka.
The brown-and-white puppies spend most of their time sleeping and nursing.
"They are just opening their eyes and their ears," Pirjo Koskinen, a Yle science journalist behind the idea for _Pentulive_, told _The Associated Press_.
"They are taking their first clumsy steps."
The livestream is letting viewers follow the puppies as they grow.
Yle also holds online chats three times a week, and has a podcast about how the pups are growing.
The show is now in its sixth season and is still very popular.
In less than two weeks, the livestream received more than 6 million views on social media alone in Finland.
Watching the puppies is good for people, too.
Koskinen said watching them hurry to their mother for milk, for example, can increase levels of a hormone called oxytocin in the human brain.
Also known as the "love hormone," it can help people feel closer to others and less anxious.
For many viewers, though, the show simply offers a break from all the stressful news we see every day.
One look at those little tails and pink noses and it's hard not to smile, said Jyri Loikkanen from Yle.
_Pentulive_ is an example of "slow TV", which focuses on long, quiet broadcasts of everyday events.
This style of TV began in Norway in 2009 with a seven-hour train journey shown minute by minute and has since become popular in other countries.

articles.title: Money-Smart Friends Could Save You $500 a Year

articles.title: Some Shinkansen Tickets to Increase in Price in 2027
articles.intro: This lesson discusses the planned price increases for some Shinkansen (bullet train) tickets in Japan starting in 2027 due to inflation.

sentences.text: Japan's bullet trains — the Shinkansen — are known for being fast, comfortable and convenient.
But passengers may soon have to pay more to travel on them.
Central Japan Railway Company (JR Central) and West Japan Railway Company (JR West) have announced plans to increase the prices of some tickets in 2027.
The Nozomi and Mizuho trains are Japan's fastest bullet trains, making the fewest stops between their starting and ending stations.
During busy periods, passengers can only buy tickets for these trains if they pay for reserved seats.

From July 2027, tickets for reserved seats will increase by between 10 yen — about 6 cents — and {{prn:880|eight hundred and eighty}} yen — about {{prn:$5.60|five dollars and sixty cents}} — depending on the route.
For example, the route between Tokyo Station and Shin-Osaka Station will increase by 700 yen, or about {{prn:$4.40|four dollars and forty cents}}.
The new price will be {{prn:6,510 |six thousand five hundred and ten}} yen, or about {{prn:$41|forty one dollars}}.

And reserved seats on the train between Tokyo and Nagoya will increase to  {{prn:11,880|eleven thousand eight hundred and eighty}} yen — about {{prn:$75|seventy five dollars}} — up from {{prn:11,300|eleven thousand and three hundred}} yen, or about {{prn:$71|seventy one dollars}}.
JR Central and JR West also plan to increase ticket prices for their first-class seats — Green Car seats — in December 2027.
Green Car tickets on Nozomi trains between Tokyo and Shin-Osaka will increase by {{prn:3,700|three thousand and seven hundred}} yen, or about {{prn:$23.40|twenty three dollars and forty cents}}.
They'll rise by {{prn:4,080 |four thousand and eighty}} yen, or about {{prn:$25.70|twenty five dollars and seventy cents}}, on Mizuho trains between Shin-Osaka and Hakata.
The companies say the price increases are needed to cover higher operating costs caused by inflation, and to keep making improvements to their services.

Tokyo company Intage Healthcare asked people in Japan questions about what they do when they get sick.

Participants were given a list of 32 conditions and, for each condition, were asked how likely they were to visit a doctor if they had symptoms.
Eighty-four percent of participants said they would go to the doctor if they had a high fever.

Many said they take OTC medicine because it helps them feel better, while others said it's because they often have it at home and it's easier and quicker than going to the doctor.

Many buy lunch at shops and restaurants less often, or choose cheaper food.
And 21% now say they look for meals or snacks provided by their company — 38% more than said so in 2025.

articles.title: What Would You Trust AI to Do for You?
articles.intro: This lesson explores global attitudes toward trusting AI, based on a survey about comfort levels and the limits of relying on artificial intelligence.

sentences.text: Asking AI to help write an email is one thing.
Handing it your money and saying, "Go shopping"?
That might take a little more trust.
A global survey of 11,000 people by Talker Research looked at where people draw the line when it comes to trusting AI.
It found that 66% were comfortable using AI in their personal lives and at work.
And on average, respondents said they knowingly used AI around six times a week.
They were most comfortable using it for general learning, such as finding out about a hobby or learning what a book is about.
They also felt comfortable using it for DIY projects, writing emails and creating pictures for fun.
But what about letting AI make decisions on its own?
Just 31% of respondents said they were likely to trust it to do this — for example, by choosing things to buy or making appointments for them.
That figure was highest in India, at 70%!
Across the survey, respondents said they would let AI spend an average of $200 to buy something without checking with them first.
When it came to dealing with companies, people wanted to know if AI was involved.
For 56%, this was more important than getting the fastest, most accurate result.
If respondents thought a company was using AI without telling them, 39% would be more careful about sharing personal information.
One in five said they would leave its website immediately.
AI did not always act in a trustworthy way, either.
In fact, 40% had caught it giving wrong or made-up information at least once.
Even so, 43% said they trusted AI more than they did a year ago.

articles.title: 59% of Americans Get Their News from Social Media
articles.intro: Explore how social media has become a main news source in the US, the rise of independent creators, and changing public trust in news.

sentences.text: Where do you go when you want to find out what's happening in the world?
Do you watch the evening news on TV, read a newspaper or look at your phone?
For many people in the US, the answer is social media — and YouTube is especially popular for political news.
Researchers from Syracuse University in New York state surveyed 1,001 Americans.
They found that 59% use social media for news "often" or "always," while 55% say they get political information from social media "often" or "always."
YouTube was found to be the most popular source for political news, with 16.5% of people choosing it as their main source.
TV came close behind at 16.1%, followed by online and print news websites at 15.7%.
People who report the news on social media are often not trained journalists — so the researchers also wanted to see how people feel about independent news creators.
They found that 61% of Americans trust well-known creators as much as trained journalists or big news companies.
However, more than three-quarters still believe there is an important difference between independent creators and trained journalists.
The survey also found that people who often use social media for news are more likely to trust independent creators.
Most of those surveyed also said they are more likely to trust an independent creator if they correct themselves online when they make a mistake.

articles.title: How to Carve the Perfect Halloween Pumpkin
articles.intro: Learn about the history and step-by-step process of carving the perfect Halloween pumpkin, including helpful tips and tricks.

sentences.text: The tradition of carving a scary face in a pumpkin is believed to have been started by Irish immigrants in the US — who, when in Ireland, would carve scary faces on turnips.
The idea was that the faces would frighten away spirits.
But how do you carve the perfect pumpkin?
First, get a large, fresh pumpkin with a flat bottom.
You can buy it early, but don't carve it until about three days before Halloween.
Start by cutting a big hole in the top with a sharp knife.
Cut at an angle, so the cut piece doesn't fall into the pumpkin when you put it back on.
Some people prefer to cut the bottom, saying it's safer to put a pumpkin over a lit candle than to put your hand inside to light it.
Then, use a big spoon to take out the soft inside of the pumpkin.
To make it easier to carve, it's best to make the pumpkin wall thinner on one side — _Good Housekeeping_ recommends leaving it about 3 centimeters thick.
You could also use the wall parts to make soup, or cook the seeds for a snack.
Next, draw a face on the pumpkin using a pen, then cut it out with a knife.
You could also draw your idea on paper first, then use a fork to make holes in the pumpkin along the lines you want to cut.
Finally, put a light inside — an artificial candle is usually safest.
If your pumpkin starts looking tired before October 31, you can put its face in cold water for a few hours to make it look fresh again.
